/-!
# Erdős Problem 403

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/403](https://www.erdosproblems.com/403)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
  number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Li76] Lin, S., *On two problems of Erdős concerning sums of distinct factorials*.
  Bell Laboratories internal memorandum (1960).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos403

/--
Does the equation
$$2^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$$
with $a_1<a_2<\cdots <a_k$ have only finitely many solutions?

Asked by Burr and Erdős. Frankl and Lin [Li76] independently showed that the answer is yes, and
the largest solution is
$$2^7=2!+3!+5!.$$
In fact Lin showed that the largest power of $2$ which can divide a sum of distinct factorials
containing $2$ is $2^{254}$, and that there are only 5 solutions to $3^m=a_1!+\cdots+a_k!$
(when $m=0,1,2,3,6$).

See also [404].

A solution is encoded below as a pair $(m, s)$ where $s$ is the finite set
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\}$ of positive integers, so the distinctness of the $a_i$ is
given by set membership. The empty set contributes no solutions since $2^m \geq 1 > 0$.

The linked proof gives more than finiteness: it classifies the solutions outright, as
$(0,\{1\})$, $(1,\{2\})$, $(3,\{2,3\})$, $(5,\{2,3,4\})$ and $(7,\{2,3,5\})$, so the set below
has exactly five elements.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/f8a51976fd2e66a52b4928c109fb9ae877a1a507/problems/403/Erdos403.lean"]
theorem erdos_403 : answer(True) ↔
    {p : ℕ × Finset ℕ | (∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a) ∧
      2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos403

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether 2^m = a_1! + ... + a_k! with a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_k has only finitely many solutions. It does not say whether a_1 = 0 or k = 0 is allowed. The Lean counts pairs (m, s) with s : Finset ℕ, and it adds the condition `∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a`, so every a_i must be positive. m ranges over all of ℕ, including m = 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument:
(i) Encoding: strictly increasing tuples (a_1 < ... < a_k) correspond one-to-one to finite sets {a_1, ..., a_k}; sorting a set recovers the tuple. The sum Σ a_i! equals Σ_{a∈s} a!, so the source's solutions and the Lean set match one-to-one, and finiteness carries over. The empty tuple or set is never a solution in either version, because 0 ≠ 2^m.
(ii) Positivity is only a convention, needed because 0! = 1! = 1. Suppose a = 0 were allowed. The extra solutions are then exactly (0,{0}), (2,{0,1,2}), and (m, {0,1} ∪ t) for each positive solution (m, {2} ∪ t) with 2 ∉ t, since 0!+1! = 2!. A mod-2 argument (0 ∈ s, 1 ∉ s) and a mod-8 argument (0,1,2 ∈ s) rule out everything else. So the set stays finite either way.
In a scratch file I proved `{p : ℕ × Finset ℕ | 2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite ↔ {p | (∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a) ∧ 2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite`, with axioms only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. Both sides are proved true; the positive side uses the linked classification.
(iii) If the source meant m ≥ 1, the only solution dropped is 2^0 = 1!.
Under every one of these readings the answer is 'yes, finitely many', which is what `answer(True)` states.

review.notes:
No findings.

**Source.** erdosproblems.com/403 asks: "Does the equation 2^m=a_1!+⋯+a_k! with a_1<⋯<a_k have only finitely many solutions?" It records the answer as yes (Frankl; Lin [Li76]), with status "PROVED (LEAN)". The Lean elaborates to `True ↔ {p : ℕ × Finset ℕ | (∀ a ∈ p.2, 0 < a) ∧ 2 ^ p.1 = ∑ a ∈ p.2, a.factorial}.Finite`. The yes answer is on the right side of `answer(True)`; the quantifier structure and the encoding are sound; the empty set is never a solution.

**Status and formal_proof.** `research solved` together with `formal_proof using lean4` matches the source.
- The linked file (Jayyhk/erdos-lean @ f8a5197) compiles against this sandbox's Mathlib with 0 errors; the only warnings are `push_neg` deprecations.
- Its `erdos_403` depends only on [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]; there is no sorry, axiom or native_decide.
- From its classification theorem I built a proof whose type is definitionally the FC statement, checked by `rfl` against `type_of% Erdos403.erdos_403`.
- I also proved that the FC set has `ncard = 5`. This confirms the docstring's list (0,{1}), (1,{2}), (3,{2,3}), (5,{2,3,4}), (7,{2,3,5}).
- A brute-force search over all subsets of {1..14} finds exactly these five solutions.

**Docstrings.** The problem docstring copies the source text verbatim; the encoding remarks are accurate. The module reference "[Li76] … Bell Laboratories internal memorandum (1960)" looks odd: the key suggests 1976. But it copies erdosproblems.com's own reference list exactly, so it is not an FC slip. I could not check the true year (arXiv API rate-limited).

**Primary source.** I downloaded the ErGr80 scan (Graham's UCSD archive, via Wayback), but it has no text layer and no OCR tool was available, so I could not read p.79 directly. This does not affect the verdict: the formal statement gives the same answer under every plausible reading (a_i ≥ 0 or ≥ 1, m ≥ 0 or ≥ 1, k free). The positivity convention is shown immaterial in Lean; see reformulations.

**Sandbox.** The `lakefile.toml` modification and the `run/` directory in the checkout predate my session (timestamps 12:21). I did not modify anything under /opt/formal-conjectures; all experiments are in /workspace/review.
